source: Jaeggi, Buschkuehl, Jonides, Perrig (2008) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory
finding: The founding result. Dual n-back training raised matrix-reasoning scores more than no training, and more with more sessions.
numbers: N=70 (34 trained analysed, 35 controls). Groups by sessions: 8 d n=16, 12 d n=22, 17 d n=16, 19 d n=15. Trained gain d=0.65 (t(33)=5.53); controls d=0.25 (retest). Group x session F(1,67)=5.27, p<.05, partial eta2=.07. Dose effect F(3,30)=9.25. 12-day group only a trend (p=.09).
quote: The dose-responsive gain in Gf indicates that the training benefit is not a threshold phenomenon.
limits: Passive (no-contact) control. 8-day group used Raven APM, others a 10-min BOMAT. Four small studies pooled. No follow-up. Authors note regression to the mean is possible.
agent_relevance: Sets the bar: the claim was a transfer shortcut. Later work says it does not hold, so do not assume that practising a memory-like drill improves general reasoning.

source: Redick et al. (2013) No evidence of intelligence improvement after working memory training: a randomized, placebo-controlled study
finding: Large three-arm replication with an active placebo. Dual n-back and visual search groups both improved on their task. No group improved on any Gf, multitasking, WM capacity, crystallised or speed test.
numbers: 75 completers (plus 55 partial; 19 dropouts: 10 n-back, 5 visual search, 4 control). 20 sessions, pre/mid/post. Dual n-back practice effect F(19,437)=18.77, p<.01, partial eta2=.45. Power to detect a medium (f=.25) or large (f=.40) Group x Session effect >.99 (>.95 at r=.30).
quote: Despite improvements on both the dual n-back and visual search tasks ... there was no positive transfer to any of the cognitive ability tests.
limits: Young adults at two US universities; RAPM was shortened. Dropout after semester end. Aptitude-treatment test (initial ability) was run too.
agent_relevance: Trained-task gain without transfer is the normal case. Our agent should expect that drilling a sub-skill leaves general reasoning unchanged.

source: Redick et al. (2013), critique section on Jaeggi 2008 and 2010
finding: The 2008 data pool four studies with different tests and session counts. Two of four showed matrix-reasoning transfer, two did not. Groups were tiny.
numbers: Jaeggi 2008 groups n=7, 8 or 11. Jaeggi 2010 Study 2: dual n-back n=25, single n-back n=21, no-contact n=43. RAPM dual n-back d=.98 vs control d=.10; BOMAT dual n-back d=.49 vs control d=.29, and the BOMAT gain did not statistically differ from control.
limits: Secondary account of other studies, read inside the Redick paper.
agent_relevance: Warns against pooling small studies and mixed test forms. Apply to our own evals: do not pool arms that used different tests.

source: Foroughi, Monfort, Paczynski, McKnight, Greenwood (2016) Placebo effects in cognitive training
finding: Expectation alone raised Gf. People recruited with a flyer saying working memory training raises intelligence gained on matrices; people recruited with a neutral flyer did not. Both did the same training.
numbers: N=50 (25 placebo, 25 control), mean age 21.5. RAPM pre 14.72, post 15.76 (placebo, d=0.50, p<.0001); control 14.68 to 14.80 (ns). BOMAT 18.04 to 19.32 (d=0.39); control 17.92 to 18.04. Group x time: RAPM d=0.98 (p=.0013), BOMAT d=1.34 (p<.0001). Training gains did not differ by group (p=.321).
quote: we do not claim that our study revealed a population of individuals whose intelligence was truly changed
limits: Supplement table disagrees with the text, so it has errors. A gain of about 1 item is not proof of real IQ change. The study did not test whether the flyer changed effort.
agent_relevance: Placebo and demand effects can mimic transfer. When we score our agent, use matched controls and avoid cueing the expected answer.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016) Working memory training does not improve performance on measures of intelligence or other measures of far transfer
finding: Largest meta-analysis. Near transfer is real. Far transfer vanishes against treated (active) controls.
numbers: 87 publications, 145 comparisons. Verbal WM g=0.31 [0.19,0.42] (treated) vs 0.42 (untreated). Visuospatial WM g=0.28 vs 0.51. Nonverbal ability g=0.05 [-0.02,0.13] (treated, k=67) vs 0.20 [0.11,0.28] (untreated, k=53). Follow-up about 5 months: nonverbal -0.05 [-0.21,0.11], k=12.
quote: no convincing evidence of any reliable improvements
limits: Mediation: WM gain to nonverbal gain beta=-.01 (p=.86, k=26). Read the first 200,000 characters of 235,663 (the rest is mostly references).
agent_relevance: Strongest single negative result: no training-style shortcut to reasoning. Plan on gains from structure at inference time, not from practice.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016), moderators and persistence
finding: Who benefits on near transfer. Children and older adults gain more on verbal WM than adults. Learning-disorder samples gain more. Cogmed beat other programs. Near gains fade partly by 5 months.
numbers: Verbal WM follow-up: treated k=10 g=0.28 [-0.004,0.56] (ns); untreated k=13 g=0.55 [0.27,0.83]. Visuospatial treated k=9 g=0.40 [0.07,0.73]. Small adult and low-dose Gf effects (0.10, 0.13) became trivial once problem comparisons were removed.
limits: Moderator tests have low power. Many comparisons lacked treated controls.
agent_relevance: Near gains stay local to the trained format. For our agent: a gain on one task type is not evidence for another.

source: Melby-Lervag, Redick, Hulme (2016), publication bias and mediation
finding: Treated-control studies show signs of publication bias; untreated-control studies show evidential value only because the control is passive. No mediation from WM gain to reasoning gain.
numbers: p-curve: untreated z(16)=-3.41, p<.01; treated z(11)=-2.19, p=.01 (no evidential value). Mediation: verbal ability on verbal WM beta=.11, p=.19, k=29; nonverbal on visuospatial beta=.13, p=.10, k=38.
limits: Meta-regression on observational gains, not experimental mediation.
agent_relevance: The 'train WM to lift reasoning' route has no demonstrated mechanism.

source: Thompson et al. (2013) Failure of working memory training to enhance cognition or intelligence
finding: Dual n-back vs multiple-object-tracking active control vs no contact. n-back level rose a lot, but there was no transfer to Raven or other untrained tests.
numbers: About 58 participants (F(2,55)). 20 sessions of about 40 min. n-back level 3.19 to 5.1 (t(19)=9.70); MOT speed 8.8 to 14.9 deg/s. Follow-up about 187 days (range 122-252): n-back d' 1.23 pre, 2.92 post, 2.60 follow-up. Could detect d>=.27. One 2-item MOT-group gain on WAIS Matrix Reasoning failed Bonferroni.
quote: no transfer of improvement was observed to any of the non-trained measurements
limits: Sample size not stated directly. Follow-up had only 10 n-back and 11 MOT people. Higher dose (30 blocks per session) than Jaeggi 2008 (20).
agent_relevance: Trained skill persists for months but does not carry. Skill retention is not generalisation.

source: Soveri, Antfolk, Karlsson, Salo, Laine (2017) Working memory training revisited: a multi-level meta-analysis of n-back training studies
finding: n-back training moves untrained n-back tasks a lot. Other WM, Gf and cognitive control move very little.
numbers: 203 effect sizes, 33 randomized trials. n-back g=0.62 [0.44,0.81]; other WM g=0.24 [0.16,0.32]; cognitive control g=0.16 [0.05,0.27]; Gf g=0.16 [0.08,0.24]. After data screening and control analysis, Gf g=0.11 (p>.05), n-back 0.59.
limits: Authors read the transfer as task-specific. Only 5 of 38 samples were older adults.
agent_relevance: Even the most favourable n-back set gives Gf g near 0.1-0.16. Training on a drill gives a drill effect.

source: Soveri et al. (2017), moderators
finding: No dose, age or single/dual effect on transfer, and active vs passive control made no difference in the direct comparison. More sessions or the dual form do not rescue transfer.
numbers: Single n-back g=0.27 [0.18,0.37], dual 0.18 [0.11,0.26]; difference g=0.09 [-0.03,0.21], p=.139. Age g=0.03 [-0.17,0.22], p=.794. Active vs passive control g=0.03 [-0.07,0.12], p=.429 (34 effect sizes). Funnel and PEESE tests showed no bias.
limits: Mostly young adults (33 of 38 samples).
agent_relevance: Rules out the dose-response claim of Jaeggi 2008 at meta-analytic scale.

source: Au et al. (2015) Improving fluid intelligence with training on working memory: a meta-analysis
finding: The pro-transfer meta-analysis. It found a small but significant n-back effect on Gf.
numbers: 20 studies, healthy adults 18-50. Weighted g=0.24 per the paper's own notes (24 observed studies; the fail-safe note says 59 null studies would cut g to 0.07). Soveri 2017 quotes it as nonverbal g=0.15 (active), 0.26 (passive), verbal 0.04 and 0.02.
limits: Only the Springer abstract and notes page was read, not the full text. The effect shrinks with active controls.
agent_relevance: Even the supportive meta-analysis sits near 0.2 and mostly against passive controls.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training
finding: WM training in children: near transfer about 0.45 SD, far transfer about 0.12 SD. Effects shrink as design quality rises.
numbers: WM far transfer overall 0.12 [0.06,0.18]; fluid intelligence 0.11 [-0.02,0.24]; cognitive control 0.09 [-0.08,0.26]; maths 0.20 [0.03,0.36]. Near transfer 0.44 (active), 0.46 (passive).
quote: The size of the effects was inversely related to the quality of the experimental design.
limits: Typically developing children and young adolescents only. Review of three meta-analyses.
agent_relevance: Same pattern in chess and music: far transfer is weak. Do not rely on training or expertise to lift general reasoning.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017), passive vs active control
finding: Control-group type explains the gap. With active controls, music and WM far transfer fall to about zero.
numbers: Music passive 0.25 [0.17,0.34] k=64 vs active 0.03 [-0.07,0.12] k=54. WM passive 0.18 [-0.09,0.26] k=34 vs active 0.05 [-0.05,0.15] k=40. Chess 0.34 overall but the one active-control study gave 0.10.
limits: Chess evidence is thin.
agent_relevance: Always report active-control arms for our scaffold gains.

source: Gobet and Sala (2022/23) Cognitive training: a field in search of a phenomenon
finding: Second-order meta-analysis: far transfer from cognitive training is null once bias and active controls are handled.
numbers: 14 independent meta-analyses, 332 samples, 1,555 effect sizes, 21,968 participants. Far transfer uncorrected g 0.04-0.19 (grand mean 0.12); corrected, active controls g -0.03 to 0.02 (grand mean 0.00). WM training placebo effect 0.15-0.20 SD; publication bias 0.05-0.10.
quote: The overall effect of far transfer is null
limits: Review with a strong stance. The call to stop far-transfer work is contested. Read the first 100,000 of 147,240 characters.
agent_relevance: Closes the question for our design: no shortcut through training-like drills. Build the scaffold, not a trained skill.

source: Brehmer, Westerberg, Backman (2012) Working-memory training in younger and older adults: training gains, transfer, and maintenance
finding: Cogmed training with an active low-level practice control. Adaptive training gave bigger gains on trained WM tasks. Reasoning (Raven) and Stroop improved equally in both groups.
numbers: N=100: adaptive 55 (29 young, 26 old), low-level practice 45 (26 young, 19 old). 5 weeks, at least 20 sessions, 3-month follow-up. Far transfer only for sustained attention (PASAT) and self-rated everyday function (CFQ).
limits: Exact effect sizes were not extracted. The CFQ gain may be an expectancy effect.
agent_relevance: Equal Raven gains in both arms indicate retest or engagement effects, not a training effect. Our harness needs an active control arm.

source: Harrison, Shipstead, Hicks, Hambrick, Redick, Engle (2013) Working memory training may increase working memory capacity but not fluid intelligence
finding: Complex-span training improved similar span tasks with new materials but not fluid intelligence.
numbers: No numbers read (abstract only, via Europe PMC).
limits: Abstract-only.
agent_relevance: Another near-yes, far-no case with a different trained task, so the null is not specific to dual n-back.

source: Richey, Phillips, Schunn, Schwartz (2014) Is the link from working memory to analogy causal? No analogy improvements following working memory training gains
finding: A test of whether the WM-reasoning correlation is causal. WM tasks improved a lot; analogy did not.
numbers: 25 trained (10 sessions of complex WM), 29 controls. Spatial CWM 3.08 to 6.44 (d=3.16); verbal CWM 4.92 to 8.80 (d=1.93); digit span d=0.69; verbal analogy .55 to .54 (d=0.10); visual analogy .77 vs .76 (d=0.05). WM change vs analogy r<=.17. Pre-training r=.46 and .51.
quote: we found no effects on analogical reasoning
limits: Power only .67-.74 for d=0.5. Seven trained participants excluded for an experimenter error.
agent_relevance: Capacity correlates with reasoning across people, but raising it does not raise reasoning. Do not treat the correlation as a lever.

source: Shipstead, Redick, Engle (2012) Is working memory training effective? A meta-analytic review
finding: Early critical review, cited by all later meta-analyses.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only the citation was confirmed through Soveri 2017 and Redick 2013.
agent_relevance: Background only.

source: Gong, Wan, Wang (2023/24) Working memory capacity of ChatGPT: an empirical study (AAAI 2024)
finding: n-back works on LLMs. ChatGPT d-prime falls as n rises, with capacity near 3. Per-trial feedback did not extend capacity.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo, n=1-3, 24 trials per block (8 match), 50 blocks per n. Verbal base d' vs 1: 1-back p<.001, 2-back p about 1.9e-5, 3-back p about .048. Spatial: 2-back p=.94, 3-back p=.97. Feedback verbal 2-back p=.25, 3-back p=.68. GPT-4 above 1 at all n (p<.001). Seven 6-13B models never above 1. Kruskal-Wallis across n H=97.5.
quote: We discover that ChatGPT has limited working memory capacity, and that its capacity limit is similar to that of humans.
limits: Feedback and CoT effects were tested against d'=1, not against baseline. Dual n-back not covered. The estimate near 3 is marginal.
agent_relevance: LLMs have a capacity cliff. In-context feedback, the nearest LLM analogue of training, did not lift the limit.

source: Gong and Zhang (2024) Self-attention limits working memory capacity of transformer-based models
finding: Small transformers trained from scratch on n-back lose accuracy as n grows. Attention entropy rises with n, a candidate mechanism.
numbers: 1-layer 1-head model: Kruskal-Wallis H=38.5, p<.001, eps2=.248. 1 vs 2: U=1825, r=-.46; 1 vs 3: r=-.68. 50 models per N, 10 epochs, 800 train and 200 test sequences per N, N=1-6. Larger models above 95% with a slight decline.
quote: suggesting that the dispersion of attention scores might be the cause of the capacity limit
limits: No entropy-accuracy correlation reported. Toy models; no fine-tuning study of capacity.
agent_relevance: The limit comes from attention spread. Drilling does not obviously remove it. External memory is the lever.

source: Zhang, Jian, Ouyang, Vosoughi (2024) Working memory identifies reasoning limits in language models (EMNLP 2024, pp. 16896-16922)
finding: n-back across models from text-ada-001 to GPT-4 shows a working-memory gap versus humans. Prompts built from error analysis (CoT+) beat standard prompting.
numbers: Models: ada, babbage, curie, davinci-001/002, gpt-3.5, gpt-4. One changed phrase raised text-ada-001 on Tracking Shuffled Objects to 25.4% (+15.8 points over CoT). A code-style rewrite raised text-davinci-002 to 96.4% (+4.8 points) on a logic task.
limits: Per-model charts were not readable from the text. Prompt gains are task-specific and CoT+ came from hand error correction.
agent_relevance: Supports scaffolding over scale: change the format of the working-memory load, as the schema does.

source: Hu and Lewis (2024) Do language models understand the cognitive tasks given to them?
finding: Poor LLM n-back may reflect misreading the task, not capacity. Weak models act as if the task were m-back with smaller m. Demos and curricula in context rescued larger models.
quote: the poor performance is due at least in part to a limitation in task comprehension and task set maintenance.
limits: Open-weight models plus GPT-3.5 only. The log-probability test is indirect.
agent_relevance: Part of the 'capacity limit' is task-set maintenance, fixed by in-context structure and not by weights. Matches our scaffold approach.

source: Strong memory, weak control: an empirical study of executive functioning in LLMs (2025)
finding: On classic span tasks open LLMs match or beat humans. Backward span, card sorting and flanker are weak. Reasoning models fix flanker but not working memory or card sorting.
numbers: 6 instruct models (Gemma-2 9B/27B, Llama-3.1 8B/70B, Qwen2 7B/72B) plus 3 reasoning models, 30 prompt permutations. Forward span of 50 digits 0.99-1.00. Backward span of 15: Gemma-9B 0.21, Llama-8B 0.18, Qwen2-7B 0.00, Llama-70B 0.83. WCST 0.29-0.53 vs humans about 0.77. Flanker incongruent 40-60% vs 93-96%; Llama-8B reasoning 0.471 to 0.910. Params vs mean span r=0.82.
limits: Small model sample; behavioural only. Reasoning traces often did not finish in 30,000 tokens.
agent_relevance: Storage is cheap; manipulation and control are weak. Put weight on control operators and checks, not more memory.

source: Aichberger and Hochreiter (2026) Unlocking the working memory of large language models for latent reasoning
finding: Trains fixed memory-block tokens as working memory for latent reasoning. It matches latent-reasoning baselines. This is architecture training with step supervision, not a human-style drill.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Abstract page only.
agent_relevance: Training a memory scaffold into a model can work, but only with supervision aimed at the target task, not by generic drilling.

source: Redick et al. (2013), individual differences and strategy in dual n-back gains
finding: Trained n-back level varied a lot between people (one reached n=10, another n=4 of 24 trainees; visual search max levels also spread widely). High and low gainers named similar strategies such as chunking and visualisation. Even large practice gains did not predict transfer.
numbers: 24 dual n-back trainees; practice effect F(19,437)=18.77, partial eta2=.45; one subject reached level 12 in visual search, another asymptoted at 6.
limits: Self-reported strategies from an open-ended question; no strategy manipulation.
agent_relevance: Gains come from task-specific strategy (chunking), which is what the schema should supply directly rather than hoping practice builds it.
